item.title: Olfactory network variability is associated with odor identification and cognitive performance in mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundOdor identification impairment is an early marker of Alzheimer's disease pathology and predicts dementia conversion in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). However, the pathophysiological role of dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) variability within olfactory networks remains unclear.ObjectiveTo characterize seed-based dFC variability across olfactory pathways in MCI with odor identification impairment (MCI-OII) and examine its associations with olfactory and cognitive performance.MethodsNinety-seven patients with MCI were recruited and subdivided into MCI-OII and those without odor identification impairment (MCI-NOII), along with 97 age-matched healthy controls (HC). All participants underwent neuropsychological assessment, olfactory testing, and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Seed-based dFC variability was computed using a sliding window approach. Correlation and exploratory mediation analyses examined associations among abnormal dFC, odor identification, and cognition.ResultsCompared to MCI-NOII and HC, MCI-OII exhibited increased dFC variability between the left piriform cortex/right insula and right caudate nucleus, and between the left insula and left middle frontal gyrus. For the connection between the left insula and left cerebellar lobule VI, dFC variability showed a graded pattern from MCI-OII to HC to MCI-NOII. Increased caudate-centered dFC variability was associated with poorer odor identification, memory, and executive performance. Furthermore, exploratory mediation analyses suggested indirect associations involving odor identification, caudate-centered dFC variability, and memory or executive function.ConclusionsMCI-OII is characterized by increased olfactory-network dFC variability, particularly in caudate-centered pathways. These findings suggest that dFC variability may serve as a candidate network-level marker of concurrent olfactory impairment and cognitive dysfunction in MCI.

item.title: MRI Microscopic Fractional Anisotropy Differences in Genetic Frontotemporal Degeneration.
item.description:
Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
BACKGROUND: In genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD), cortical and subcortical brain volume differences have been detected using volumetric MRI decades before symptoms appear. Microscopic fractional anisotropy (μFA) is a diffusion MRI metric that is sensitive to diffusion anisotropy regardless of relative fiber orientations within a voxel and is more accurate than conventional DTI metrics for detecting age-related microstructural changes in healthy individuals and differences in some neurological diseases. PURPOSE: To compare μFA, mean diffusivity (MD), and volume between genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD) variant carriers and non-carriers in the insula, frontal pole, and medial orbitofrontal cortex. STUDY TYPE: Cross-sectional cohort study. POPULATION: Carriers of FTD variants in C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT (n = 12; age = 56.7 ± 8.12 years; 50% female) and familial non-variant carriers (n = 8; age = 59.5 ± 10.3 years; 62.5% female). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3T; Magnetization prepared rapid acquisition with gradient echoes (MPRAGE) sequence (anatomical imaging) and a diffusion echo-planar imaging sequence with modified diffusion gradients for spherical tensor encoding (μFA measurement). ASSESSMENT: MPRAGE images underwent cortical and subcortical segmentation to obtain regions of interest. MD and μFA maps were derived from diffusion MRI data. μFA, MD, and volumes were compared between FTD variant carriers (n = 5 symptomatic, and n = 7 asymptomatic) and familial non-carriers. STATISTICAL TESTS: Linear models with heteroscedasticity-consistent confidence intervals were computed to analyze between-group differences in outcomes while controlling for age (alpha = 0.05). RESULTS: FTD variant carriers exhibited significantly lower insula μFA than non-carriers (η2p = 0.22). Post hoc contrasts showed significantly reduced insula μFA in symptomatic carriers compared to non-carriers (d = 1.57). Mean μFA in asymptomatic carriers (mean ± standard error (SE): 0.454 ± 0.010) was not significantly different to that in non-carriers (mean ± SE: 0.471 ± 0.009, p = 0.465), nor in symptomatic carriers (mean ± SE: 0.430 ± 0.012, p = 0.290). DATA CONCLUSION: μFA is reduced in the insula, a region vulnerable to early atrophy in FTD, reflecting microstructural changes in genetic FTD with greater effect sizes than MD and volume. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 2.

item.title: Sentence-level neural dynamics in speech motor cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Prior recordings from speech motor cortex have revealed phonemic, syllabic, articulatory and speech-sequence representations, while more recent studies indicate that activity may also reflect higher-order features of speech production. However, whether speech motor cortex is sensitive to the linguistic organization of sentences remains unclear. Here we show that single-unit activity in speech motor cortex contains information about sentence-level linguistic structure. In three BrainGate2 participants with implanted microelectrode arrays in the left precentral gyrus, we recorded neural activity during an instructed-delay speech task comprising English sentences, word lists, syntactically structured nonword sentences and nonword lists. Neural activity in areas 6v and 55b contained speech- and language-related components, with stronger stimulus-condition effects in 55b, and stimulus condition was decodable in all three participants. In two larger datasets, semantic categories of English sentences were decodable from neural activity. These findings demonstrate that speech motor cortex encodes information about linguistic structure and semantic content at the level of sentences.

item.title: The extended default mode network dysconnectivity in schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The default mode network (DMN) extends beyond cortex into subcortical structures, yet how this extended DMN (eDMN) is causally reorganized in schizophrenia (SZ) remains unclear. Here, resting-state fMRI from 74 healthy controls (HC) and 66 SZ patients was analyzed. Subject-specific eDMNs were identified using spatially-constrained independent component analysis, and effective connectivity among 13 regions was estimated with spectral dynamic causal modeling, with group effects assessed using parametric empirical Bayes. Causal centrality—a dynamics-sensitive and causality-based measure of nodal importance—was computed per region, compared between groups, and correlated with MATRICS cognitive scores in patients. Causal centrality rankings were highly similar across groups (ρ = 0.87), with both favoring subcortical over cortical regions. Group differences were regionally specific: temporal cortex was more causally central in patients, whereas posterior parietal cortex was more causally central in controls. Most connection-level SZ-HC differences originated from ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, prefrontal cortex, basal forebrain, temporal cortex, and thalamus. In patients, temporal causal centrality correlated negatively with reasoning/problem-solving, and ventrolateral prefrontal causal centrality with processing speed and composite cognition. The eDMN's core causal architecture is preserved in schizophrenia, but temporal influence is enhanced and parietal influence attenuated—alterations that are behaviorally meaningful and consistent with pathological reorganization.

item.title: DECODE: DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States: Separating Structure-Coupled and Structure-Decoupled Functional Organization in Alzheimers Disease
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Brain functional activity emerges within an underlying structural scaffold. While structural network connectivity provides a relatively stable anatomical backbone for large-scale communication, functional interactions are high-dimensional and temporally dynamic, forming recurrent patterns that can be represented in a latent space of transient functional states. Yet, how these transient functional states are organized and the extent to which they remain constrained by structural network connectivity or become relatively decoupled from structural organization over time remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce DECODE (DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States), a data-driven latent-space framework that uses independent component analysis (ICA) and multimodal data to decompose resting-state dynamic functional network connectivity into a lower-dimensional representation of transient functional states. These states capture temporally varying structure-coupled and structure-decoupled patterns using diffusion MRI-derived structural network connectivity priors. Structure-coupled states reflect functional configurations more strongly anchored to major structural motifs, whereas structure-decoupled states represent configurations less constrained by the identified structural organization, while potentially remaining within structurally defined dynamical bounds. DECODE identifies reproducible structure-coupled and structure-decoupled states, with mean squared error reconstruction of dynamic information < 0.1 and adjusted R-squared = 0.4. Applied to Alzheimers disease (AD), DECODE revealed stronger group differences (FDR-corrected p-value 0.05) in both connectivity organization and temporal dynamics for decoupled states. These findings suggest that functional states less constrained by identified structural organization may be more vulnerable to AD-related disruption, whereas structure-coupled states may be relatively preserved. More broadly, DECODE provides a reproducible and generalizable framework for quantifying how functional dynamics are shaped by, or diverge from, structural organization by incorporating a latent representation of the structural connectome as an informative prior. Our findings established structural and functional alignment variation by distinguishing dynamic functional patterns closely coupled with structure from those that deviate from it.

item.title: Environmental Exposures and Brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging Phenotypes in Cognitively Healthy Ageing: A Systematic Review
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Air pollution and built environment features are increasingly associated with negative health outcomes, yet their relation to brain health in cognitively healthy older adults remains unclear. Methods: To synthesise the extant literature, we conducted a systematic review, searching MEDLINE (PubMed) and Web of Science (Core Collection) from inception to February 23, 2026. Eligible studies assessed a natural or built environmental exposure against brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures in cognitively healthy older adults (ages 65+). Reviewers screened and extracted summary data from published reports in Covidence; no individual patient data were sought. The main outcome was brain health; findings were synthesised narratively using an effect-direction approach, as heterogeneous exposures, outcomes, and effect metrics precluded pooling. Findings: Of 2,496 records screened, 27 studies met eligibility, comprising >84,000 older adults across 10 countries: United States, South Korea, United Kingdom, France, Spain, Sweden, Netherlands, Taiwan, Germany, and Japan. Thirteen studies were cross-sectional and 14 were cohort studies (nine observational and five longitudinal). Higher air pollution exposure—particularly PM2.5, NO2, and PM10—was associated with altered brain structure: smaller total, grey matter, and white matter volumes, greater white matter hyperintensities, cortical thinning, and smaller medial temporal and hippocampal volumes; greenspace was associated with more favourable brain structure in several mostly cross-sectional studies, though findings were not uniform. Thirteen studies met criteria for high methodological quality and low though not uniform risk of bias; outcome assessment was a recurring source of bias (12 of 27 studies), and four of the five longitudinal studies did not meet criterion for follow-up adequacy.Interpretation: This review synthesises emerging observational evidence that air pollution is associated with differences in brain structure in cognitively healthy ageing. Because the included evidence is predominantly cross-sectional, these associations are hypothesis generating; if confirmed in longitudinal studies, this modifiable exposure could serve as a potential target for policymakers aiming to protect brain health in the fastest growing segment of the global population.

item.title: From the app to the lexicon: Neurocognitive markers of word integration in a second language
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The consolidation of newly learned vocabulary into semantic memory networks is a critical process in word learning, including second-language (L2) acquisition. However, most neurocognitive studies of lexical-semantic integration rely on short, artificial learning paradigms, leaving open the question of whether naturalistic, app-based learning produces comparable neural outcomes. In this study, we combined an ecological learning environment with controlled electrophysiological testing to examine whether vocabulary learned through Duolingo shows neural signatures of semantic integration. Native Spanish speakers studied Guarani vocabulary for five weeks and subsequently completed a semantic decision task during EEG recording that included both L1 (Spanish) and L2 (Guarani) word pairs. Critically, L2 targets were classified as remote (learned earlier during the five-week training and not practiced in the final stage) or recent (learned in the final training stage and tested approximately 10 days later), allowing us to assess consolidation-related differences. Behaviorally, participants responded more accurately and faster to L1 than L2 words, and accuracy for related items was higher for remotely than recently learned items, consistent with consolidation-related strengthening. Electrophysiologically, robust N400 priming effects emerged for remotely learned words—whereas no facilitation was observed for recent words. This graded pattern suggests that only words with extended consolidation time exhibited neural markers of lexical–semantic integration. Together, these findings demonstrate that combining real-world digital learning with controlled neural testing can reveal how naturalistic language experience shapes the neurocognitive dynamics of word learning and consolidation.

item.title: Neural evidence for intact statistical learning in Developmental Dyslexia in the absence of conclusive behavioral results: an individual differences approach to cognitive correlates
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Individual differences in Statistical Learning (SL) are associated with reading ability, yet evidence on whether SL is impaired in Developmental Dyslexia (DD) is inconsistent. Furthermore, DD is associated with impairments in Rhythmic Ability (RA) and Working Memory (WM). This study examined SL in adults with self-reported diagnoses of DD compared to Typical Readers (TR), and explored whether individual differences in RA, WM, and vocabulary related to individual SL ability in speech segmentation.A total of 143 participants (N_DD = 25, N_TR = 118) were exposed to an artificial language of trisyllabic nonsense-words while neural entrainment to the words assessed SL via electroencephalography (EEG), followed by behavioral SL outcome measures. Aiming to assess individual differences, we linked the neural measure of SL to a battery of tests measuring musicality, RA, WM, and vocabulary size. Results indicated neural evidence for SL in both groups, with similar neural entrainment to the structure during exposure. Behavioral performance in the DD group on SL seemed below TR, though Bayesian analyses rendered this inconclusive. The DD group obtained lower scores on tasks measuring RA, WM and vocabulary size, which was primarily driven by the latter two. Comparison of relations between neural SL and these tasks indicated no group differences therein. Exploratively combining the groups into one population resulted in anecdotal Bayesian evidence that individual differences in SL related to WM and RA measured by sensorimotor synchronization, which was rendered inconclusive in sensitivity analyses. Our results emphasize the importance of an individual differences approach, moving beyond group comparisons.

item.title: Allometric scaling of resting-state EEG network topography across childhood and adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Brain network topography undergoes complex reorganization throughout childhood and adolescence. Quantifying the functional form of this maturation remains a key challenge. Here, we applied developmental allometry to sensor-level resting-state EEG networks from 1,957 participants aged 5–21 years (Healthy Brain Network). We fitted power laws of age to four graph-theoretic indices (small-worldness, global and local efficiency, modularity) across five frequency bands. Nineteen of the 20 band-by-index exponents were negative. Low-frequency (delta and theta) small-worldness showed the steepest declines (alpha = -0.878 and − 0.868), indicating a near-halving of the metric with each doubling of age. Lobe-resolved analyses revealed a pan-lobar but non-uniform decline, with posterior regions showing steeper age-related changes than frontal regions in specific bands. While raw-space cross-validation did not uniquely favor the power law over linear models, its scale-free exponent provides a unified parameter to compare developmental rates across spatial and spectral scales. Individual deviations from this topology did not track dimensional psychopathology. These exponents provide a quantitative reference for EEG network topography maturation and highlight the necessity of frequency- and region-specific modeling.

item.title: A realistic model of resting-state BOLD spectra in white matter
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Resting-state BOLD signals in white matter show a spectral elevation near 0.06 Hz on an exponentially decaying background, and white-matter hemodynamic response functions (HRFs) have a prominent initial dip. We model the resting signal as shot noise: randomly timed neural events are filtered by the HRF, so that the spectrum is the input spectrum multiplied by the squared HRF gain, plus instrumental noise. The initial dip and post-stimulus undershoot remove low-frequency power, making the white-matter HRF a band-pass filter with maximum gain near 0.05 Hz. One set of physiological parameters fits both a measured white-matter HRF (R² = 0.993) and the group-mean white-matter spectrum (R² = 0.987), with a resting transit time of about 4 s and a metabolic response weighted about twice as heavily as in gray matter. Deepening the dip raises the filter gain and moves its maximum toward 0.06 Hz, linking the dip to the spectral feature. A narrower line in individual spectra is reproduced either by an underdamped HRF that matches the measured response over its first 20 s or by a rhythmic input near 0.06 Hz. The model identifies which HRF properties could explain the decline of the peak with age.

item.title: Opposite Modulations of Thalamo-Cingulate and Fronto-IFOF Gray-White Matter Circuits Underlie Symptomatic and Cognitive Gains with Magnetic Seizure Therapy in Schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Magnetic seizure therapy (MST) has shown promise for treating schizophrenia, but the functional brain changes associated with its clinical and cognitive outcomes remain unclear. We investigated gray matter–white matter (GM–WM) functional connectivity and its associations with symptom and cognitive changes following MST. Fifty-three patients with schizophrenia and 40 demographically matched healthy controls underwent baseline resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging; 33 patients with usable pretreatment and post-treatment imaging data were included in longitudinal analyses. Functional connectivity was compared between groups and across treatment time points, and connectivity changes were examined in relation to clinical and cognitive changes. Following MST, patients showed reductions in psychotic symptoms and improvements in the MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery composite score and processing speed. Treatment-related connectivity changes predominantly involved GM–WM connections. Decreased connectivity within a thalamus–corona radiata–cingulate circuit was associated with symptom improvement, whereas increased connectivity involving the left inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and frontal regions was associated with cognitive improvement. Exploratory atlas-based analyses identified spatial associations between functional connectivity patterns and normative histaminergic and serotonergic receptor distributions, including 5-HT4 receptor maps. These findings suggest that symptom and cognitive improvements following MST are associated with changes in GM–WM functional connectivity. The receptor mapping results provide an exploratory neurochemical context for these associations, rather than evidence of treatment-induced changes in neurotransmitter levels or receptor availability.

item.title: Cross-Condition Transfer Learning for EEG-Based Inner Speech Classification: A Controlled Evaluation of Neural Networks and Temporal Segmentation
item.description:
[预印本] Preprints.org
Transferring a decoder trained on overt (pronounced) speech to inner speech has been proposed to offset scarce inner-speech EEG. This was re-examined on the “Thinking out loud” dataset (ds003626, 10 participants, four words), with no test trial in training or selection. EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, CSP+LDA and a Riemannian tangent-space pipeline were compared on bidirectional transfer, combined training, overt pre-training with fine-tuning on 25–100% inner-speech subsets, maximum-mean-discrepancy alignment and four trial windows. Shuffled-label controls and an exploratory, post hoc test family were used. Cross-participant, held-out-session, channel, band, external-electrode and second-dataset (ds006104) arms were reference checks. Within participant, overt speech was decodable in the action interval (0.34–0.43, chance 0.250). It survived a held-out session, peaked in 30–100 Hz and did not cross participants. Two lip electrodes alone decoded the pronounced word at 0.67–0.83. Regressing the external electrodes out of the scalp reduced three decoders’ overt accuracy to 0.28–0.40, leaving a residual of undetermined origin. Inner-speech accuracy was not distinguishable from chance. No transfer method, fine-tuned or not, improved reliably on its controls. Effects below about 2–6 percentage points were likely missed. These findings suggest that articulation-related features learned from overt speech may not provide sufficiently transferable information for inner-speech decoding under the present conditions.

item.title: Disentangling the Spatiotemporal Neural Dynamics of Conflict Detection and Resolution between Lexical and Sublexical Processes in Oral Word Reading: An Intracranial SEEG Study.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Object recognition relies on correspondence between whole objects and their subcomponents. When this correspondence is disrupted, accurate recognition requires detecting conflicts and inhibiting misleading subcomponent information, yet the neural basis underlying these processes remain unclear. Written language, with sublexical components that may conflict with whole words, provides an ideal testbed. Using stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) recorded from 39 participants (both sexes) during Chinese character reading, we revealed a functional dissociation between neural systems supporting conflict detection and inhibitory control. Conflict detection was associated with β band activity in the fusiform gyrus and widespread θ and α band effects across temporal and parietal regions. Inhibitory control was associated with α and β band activity in the inferior frontal and precentral gyri. Granger causality analysis showed increased β band connectivity from conflict-processing to inhibitory-control regions under conflict conditions. These findings demonstrate that disruptions of whole-sublexical correspondence engage dissociable neural systems for conflict detection and inhibitory control, implemented through frequency- and region-specific neural oscillations and coordinated via increased information transfer from posterior to frontal regions.Significance Statement Reading often requires resolving conflicts between competing linguistic representations, yet the neural mechanisms that detect such conflicts and resolve them remain poorly understood. Using stereo-electroencephalography with millimeter-scale spatial and millisecond-scale temporal resolution, we dissociated sublexical conflict detection from inhibitory control during Chinese character reading. We show that these processes are supported by distinct low-frequency oscillatory networks and are linked through directed functional interactions. These findings move beyond traditional accounts of sublexical effects by identifying their underlying cognitive components and neural dynamics, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how cognitive control supports fluent word recognition.

item.title: Category learning drives cortical attentional gain to diagnostic dimensions of perceptual information.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Humans and other animals develop remarkable perceptual and cognitive specializations for identifying, differentiating, and acting on classes of ecologically important signals. This expertise is flexible enough to support diverse perceptual judgments: a voice, for example, simultaneously conveys what a talker says, as well as myriad cues about her identity and state. Expert perception across complex signals thus involves discovering and learning regularities that best inform diverse perceptual judgments, as well as weighting this information flexibly as task demands change. Here, we test whether this process may involve attentional gain. We use two prospective auditory category learning tasks to relate a complex, entirely novel soundscape to four classes of 'alien identity' and two classes of 'alien size.' Identity, but not size, categorization requires discovery and learning of patterned acoustic input situated in one of two simultaneous, non-overlapping frequency bands. This allows us to capitalize on the coarsely segregated, frequency-band-specific channels tiling auditory cortex. We use fMRI to ask whether category-relevant perceptual information present in one frequency band is prioritized relative to simultaneous, uninformative information in the other frequency band. Only among participants expert at alien identity categorization do we observe neural prioritization of the identity-diagnostic frequency band. This prioritization persists even when the diagnostic information becomes irrelevant in the size categorization task. Tellingly, the neural selectivity evoked implicitly in the identity categorization task aligns with that in an independent task, where activation is driven by explicit and sustained selective attention to pure tones in one or the other frequency band. Additionally, the learning trajectories taken to achieve expert-level categorization leave fingerprints on the patterns of neural activity associated with the diagnostic dimension. In all, this indicates that learning categories can drive attentional gain to category-diagnostic input dimensions.

item.title: Spontaneous Neuronal Activity in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Insights from Human and Animal Studies.
item.description:
The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
Developmental spontaneous neuronal activity (SNA) plays an instrumental role in the generation of precise brain circuits. Spontaneous activity patterns guide neuronal differentiation, synaptic refinement, and circuit formation; consequently, perturbations in these activity patterns can profoundly influence brain network organization. Growing evidence suggests that mutations in autism-associated genes lead to alterations of the SNA pattern during early brain development, thereby giving rise to the behavioral features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This review integrates findings from neuroimaging studies, which reveal widespread alterations in neuronal excitability in individuals with ASD. Regional homogeneity and functional connectivity analyses consistently demonstrate region-specific abnormalities, including hyperactivity in higher-order cortical regions, hypoactivity in sensorimotor areas, and disrupted long-range connectivity. These functional alterations are closely linked to the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms such as excitation-inhibition (E/I) imbalance, impaired GABAergic signaling, glutamatergic dysregulation, and abnormalities in calcium-dependent signaling pathways. Identification of activity-based biomarkers, together with advanced neuroimaging techniques and computational and machine learning (ML) approaches, may facilitate early diagnosis of ASD. Understanding the origin and consequences of alterations in SNA provides a unifying framework for identifying novel targets for designing pharmacological intervention strategies.

item.title: Beyond Morphology: Quantitative Bilateral Self-Referenced Frequency-Domain Diffuse Optical Spectroscopy Reveals Functional Abnormalities in Patellar Tendinopathy.
item.description:
IEEE transactions on bio-medical engineering
Patellar tendinopathy (PT) involves functional and metabolic abnormalities that may precede structural degeneration, whereas MRI and ultrasonography primarily depict morphology. To bridge this gap, we aim to develop a quantitative optical method for detecting PT-related functional and hemodynamic abnormalities. We developed an embedded multi-wavelength frequency-domain diffuse optical spectroscopy system integrating sinusoidal modulation, synchronized acquisition, real-time Goertzel demodulation, optical-property inversion, chromophore fitting, and standardized grid scanning over the patellar tendon region. To reduce inter-subject variability, a bilateral self-referenced strategy used the contralateral tendon as an endogenous reference. A composite optical biomarker, Tendon Hemodynamic Index (THI), was defined by integrating differential tissue oxygenation and blood-volume-related information. Phantom and in vivo measurements demonstrated robust quantitative performance. In a clinical cohort, THI was significantly elevated in PT patients and correlated with symptom severity and functional impairment across the full cohort, with Spearman correlations of 0.69 with the Numeric Rating Scale and -0.74 with the Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment-Patella score. In this exploratory cohort, THI distinguished PT from healthy controls with 91.8% accuracy, 95.8% sensitivity, 88.0% specificity, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.928. In imaging negative but symptom-positive cases, THI achieved 88.2% classification accuracy. In three exploratory follow-up cases, THI decreased toward the bilateral baseline as symptoms improved over 8 weeks. The proposed method enables self-referenced quantification of PT-related functional abnormalities. By revealing tendon hemodynamic abnormalities beyond structural imaging, this work supports early PT detection, objective severity assessment, and quantitative monitoring of disease recovery.

item.title: Dynamic Brain Network Transitions and Sensorimotor Performance Across the Adult Lifespan.
item.description:
Seminars in ultrasound, CT, and MR
Healthy adult aging is accompanied by subtle variations in fine sensorimotor control and cognitive flexibility. Traditional static neuroimaging approaches often overlook short-term temporal dynamics. This study investigated cross-sectional associations between temporal brain state transitions and sensorimotor performance-specifically force matching and motor learning adaptation-across the adult lifespan. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) and behavioral data from 218 healthy adults (aged 18-88 years; 99 females, 119 males) were analyzed across three age groups: young (18-35 years; n = 45; 25 females, 20 males), middle-aged (>35-60 years; n = 88; 37 females, 51 males), and older adults (>60 years; n = 85; 37 females, 48 males).Sex distribution did not differ significantly across age groups (p = 0.302). Time varying functional connectivity was modeled to extract Fractional Occupancy (FO), Mean Dwell Time (MDT), and global Switching Rate (SR) across six recurrent brain states. Behavioral metrics included finger force overcompensation (force matching) and spatial trajectory error during late-exposure motor learning. Advancing age was significantly associated with higher trajectory error during motor learning (p < 0.001) and greater force overcompensation (p ≤ 0.001). Post-hoc comparisons revealed non-linear cross-sectional differences, with older adults exhibiting higher error margins than young and middle-aged groups. Global switching rate (SR) demonstrated a statistically significant inverse association with motor learning error (β = -0.122 to -0.280, p < 0.03), indicating that higher dynamic network flexibility is associated with lower motor adaptation error. Furthermore, age was negatively correlated with switching rate (β = -0.166, p = 0.023). In the Executive Control Network (State 3), females exhibited significantly higher FO (p = 0.003) and adjusted MDT (p = 0.007) compared to males. Additionally, older males showed a nominal positive association with Task-Positive Network (State 5) dwell time (ρ = 0.204, p = 0.026). These findings suggest an age-associated pattern of "dynamic rigidity," characterized by a reduced propensity for global brain state switching within cross-sectional observations. Fluid state transition capacity-rather than isolated state occupancy-offers significant explanatory relevance for sensorimotor adaptation across the adult lifespan.

item.title: High cortical lesion burden moderates the association between brain networks and processing speed in older adults with multiple sclerosis.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Cortical lesions (CL) are common in older adults with multiple sclerosis (OAMS), but their influence on the relationship between resting-state network strength (RSNS) and cognitive function in OAMS remains underexplored. This study aimed to determine whether CL moderates associations between RSNS and processing speed in OAMS. 82 OAMS participants (mean age: 64.4 ± 4.1 years; males/females: 26/56) were scanned in a 3T scanner. Identification of CL on double inversion-recovery (DIR) MRI images in this study was performed using established consensus recommendations. We estimated functional brain networks using a data-driven procedure to extract seven intrinsic resting-state networks. The Symbol-Digit-Modalities Test (SDMT), an established test of processing speed and working memory, served as the cognitive outcome measure. Multiple linear regressions, adjusted for sociodemographic covariates, examined the relationship between RSNS and SDMT performance with CL (three levels: no CL, 1-2 CL, and ≥ 3 CL) as a moderator. Significant CL-by-network interactions in models adjusted for sociodemographic covariates and white matter lesion load indicated that high-burden CL vs. no CL moderated the association between RSNS and SDMT in the auditory network (AUD) (p = 0.030), dorsal attention network (DAN) (p = 0.033), left frontoparietal network (LFPN) (p = 0.030), and posterior DMN (pDMN) (p = 0.030). Conditional effects showed that high-burden CLs attenuated positive associations between specific brain networks and SDMT performance. These findings suggest that higher CL burden restricts the functional brain support for processing speed and working memory performance in OAMS.

item.title: Beyond sleep macrostructure: a high-definition review of acupuncture's electrophysiological signatures in modulating sleep microarchitecture (spectral power, spindles, and slow oscillations).
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Sleep science has shifted from coarse stage-based metrics toward a microstructural perspective that treats electroencephalographic biomarkers, spectral power, sleep spindles, and slow oscillations as candidate windows onto restorative brain function. This high-definition review evaluates whether acupuncture has been shown to modify these features. Direct evidence from natural overnight sleep is currently very limited: most available electrophysiological studies were conducted during quiet wakefulness, in resting daytime EEG recordings from clinical groups, or under propofol anesthesia. These studies demonstrate that acupuncture or related electrical acupoint stimulation can produce state-, region-, and frequency-dependent changes in EEG power and network organization, but they do not yet establish increased NREM spindle density, improved slow-oscillation-spindle coupling, enhanced slow-wave morphology, memory consolidation, or glymphatic clearance. We therefore distinguish directly observed findings from indirect mechanistic support and from hypotheses that require prospective testing. Plausible pathways include ascending somatosensory influences on thalamocortical excitability, autonomic and hypothalamic effects that may reduce hyperarousal, and peripheral or central neurochemical processes involving adenosine, GABA, serotonin, and BDNF; however, the causal sequence from needling to sleep microarchitecture remains unproven. Future progress requires preregistered, adequately powered, multi-night studies using validated spindle and slow-wave detectors, explicit control estimands, and multimodal measurements. Biomarker-guided and closed-loop acupuncture should presently be regarded as a research framework rather than an established treatment strategy.

item.title: Cholinergic blockade reveals a role for human hippocampal theta in memory encoding but not retrieval.
item.description:
eLife
Cholinergic dysfunction is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease and other memory disorders. Yet, the neurophysiological mechanisms linking cholinergic signaling to memory remain poorly understood. In this study, we administered scopolamine, a muscarinic cholinergic antagonist, to neurosurgical patients with intracranial electrodes as they performed an associative recognition memory task. When scopolamine was present at encoding, we observed disruptions to hippocampal slow theta oscillations (2-4 Hz), with selective impairments to recollection-based memory. However, when scopolamine was present during retrieval alone, we observed disruptions to slow theta without impaired memory performance. These disruptions included dose-dependent reductions in theta power, theta phase reset, and encoding-retrieval pattern reinstatement. Together, our results challenge the notion that theta oscillations are necessary for memory retrieval, and instead suggest that theta universally reflects an encoding-related neural state. These findings motivate updates to current models of acetylcholine's role in memory and may inform future therapies targeting rhythmic biomarkers of memory dysfunction.

item.title: Tau-vulnerable medial temporal lobe connectivity drives a functional-to-synaptic cascade in Alzheimer's disease
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Distinct tau-vulnerable and relatively spared subregions exist within the medial temporal lobe (MTL). However, it remains unclear that how functional connectivity (FC), anchored to tau-vulnerable MTL subregions, is related to tau pathology, synaptic dysfunction, and cognitive decline across the Alzheimer's disease (AD) continuum. We here probe into this with resting-state fMRI data from a discovery cohort (ADNI; N = 386; cognitively normal [CN], mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and AD; 144 with 2-year follow-up) and an independent validation cohort at local hospital (N = 100; CN, subjective cognitive decline [SCD], and MCI; 25 receiving high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation [HF-rTMS]). We first separated the MTL into subregions with high and low neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) burden based on histological atlases, and calculated the seed-based whole-brain FC for each subregion. Second, group differences were assessed using ANCOVA, and associations with amyloid-β (Aβ)/tau pathology, synaptic biomarkers, and cognitive performance were examined. Third, serial mediation, cross-lagged, and longitudinal regression analyses were performed to investigate the proposed pathological sequence, with additional evidence from HF-rTMS intervention and autopsy-confirmed Braak staging. Our results showed that, with the development of AD, FC reductions were focused on the high-NFT MTL network, particularly involving the inferior temporal gyrus and precuneus. Baseline tau burden in high-NFT MTL regions was able to predict subsequent FC alterations. Interestingly, FC between the high-NFT MTL and global brain showed region-specific associations with synaptic biomarkers, including negative associations in the cerebellum and positive associations in the precentral gyrus. We also observed a divergent association between the FC and cognition or pathology at different AD stages, shifting from positive in the early stages to negative in advanced AD. Serial mediation analyses supported a pathway linking tau burden to cognitive impairment through altered high-NFT MTL connectivity in the precuneus and occipital regions and subsequent synaptic dysfunction. Cross-lagged and longitudinal analyses further confirmed the proposed temporal sequence. Furthermore, HF-rTMS-related cognitive improvements were partially associated with enhanced synaptic plasticity through changes in precuneus-high-NFT MTL connectivity. Collectively, these findings support a spatiotemporal framework linking the dysfunction of tau-vulnerable MTL network to synaptic impairment and cognitive decline, highlighting high-NFT MTL-based FC as a potential imaging marker tracking AD progression.

item.title: Exploring subacute effects of a DMT and harmine meditation retreat on the brain's control energy landscape
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Modeling the brain as a controllable structural network allows the estimation of the control energy (CE) required to reach functional states, where low-CE states are more accessible. Psychedelics are thought to acutely flatten the brain's CE landscape, broadening the repertoire of reachable states, but whether this reorganization persists into the subacute ``afterglow" window is largely unknown. This exploratory study uses rs-fMRI from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (N = 39; 19 verum [N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) + harmine, Ayahuasca-inspired formulation], 20 placebo) scanned before and after a three-day meditation retreat. We compute CE on a group human connectome project (HCP) structural connectome under two approaches that emphasize long and short timescale dynamics. Globally, we found no systematic shift in the distribution of CE between transitions, however mean CE increased in both groups at the long timescale approach. Surviving network effects emerge when a network's intrinsic timescale matches the stabilization regime. In the long timescale regime, the central executive network (CEN) showed an increase in post-retreat CE within the verum group that survived Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR-BH) correction. Although CE and functional connectivity are distinct, this higher CEN cost may relate to the reduced within-network connectivity previously reported subacutely after psilocybin. The default mode network (DMN) also showed a post-retreat CE increase in both groups, but neither change survived FDR correction. In the short timescale approach, the visual network (VN) showed a FDR-BH CE decrease within the verum group, consistent with reduced dynamical demand in a region acutely engaged by DMT. To examine whether changes were concentrated in less accessible states, we additionally analyzed rare brain states, defined by the top decile of information content. This analysis revealed a modest session × condition interaction in the long timescale approach. Overall, the two timescale lenses surface different network effects, that align with cortical timescale hierarchies. These findings point to network- and timescale-specific, rather than global, CE changes in the afterglow window, though effects are small and heterogeneous and require confirmation in larger samples. Characterizing whether and where psychedelic effects persist into the subacute window is relevant to psychedelic-assisted therapy, including safety, therapeutic timing, and durability of drug effects. More broadly, considering cortical timescale hierarchies may help identify network-specific CE changes that might be less apparent when networks are evaluated under a single dynamical timescale.

item.title: Association Between Behavioral Activation System, White Matter Microstructure, and Depressive Symptoms in Major Depressive Disorder
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Reduced behavioral activation system (BAS) sensitivity is a core behavioral phenotype of anhedonia, a key symptom of major depressive disorder (MDD) that involves multifaceted dysfunctions in the reward processing system. However, the white matter microstructural basis of this phenotype remains unclear. We examined fractional anisotropy (FA) in 54 MDD patients and 72 healthy controls (HC) and explored relationships among FA, BAS Total scores, and depressive symptom severity (Beck Depression Inventory, BDI) in MDD patients. All participants underwent diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and completed the BDI, BAS, and Behavioral Inhibition System (BIS) scales. Tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) was used to extract FA values from seven a priori white matter tracts. Compared with HC, the MDD group showed significantly lower FA values in six tracts (right superior corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, posterior thalamic radiation, genu of corpus callosum, sagittal stratum, and fornix), as well as significantly lower BAS Total scores and higher BDI scores. Partial correlation analyses within the MDD group showed that FA values in four tracts (right superior corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, posterior thalamic radiation, and sagittal stratum) were significantly positively correlated with BAS Total scores. Mediation analyses controlling for age, sex, and BIS score revealed that BAS Total scores significantly mediated the relationship between FA values in these four tracts and BDI scores, with an indirect-only mediation pattern. When BIS was tested as an alternative mediator, none of the indirect effects were significant, supporting the specificity of the BAS-mediated pathway. These findings provide new imaging evidence for a "white matter microstructure–behavior–symptom" pathway, suggesting that targeting white matter microstructure and BAS function may help alleviate anhedonia in MDD.

item.title: Learning to Navigate a Changing World: From Brain Systems to Novel Algorithms.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Natural organisms navigate a world in constant flux and are frequently confronted with sensory ambiguity and shifting goals. While biological systems can adapt rapidly to navigate in novel and nonstationary environments, this challenge remains a significant hurdle for artificial intelligence. In this review, we examine recent progress in understanding neurobiological systems that allow for adaptive, efficient spatial and abstract navigation in dynamic environments and how these observations have informed new developments for the same behavior in machines. We highlight how predictive learning serves as a unifying framework to describe the organization of neural activity across distributed systems for navigation, including the hippocampal formation, parietal cortex, and higher-order associative structures. Specifically, we explore how such neurobiological systems encode expected future states, dynamic target trajectories, action plans, and internal behavioral strategies. Finally, we contrast the diffuse, inefficient exploration of canonical artificial agents with the structured, efficient control policies for goal-directed navigation observed in natural organisms. By grounding learning in the interplay between action, prediction, and natural behavioral statistics, navigation provides a roadmap for building resilient, neurobiologically inspired continual learning in artificial agents.

item.title: Levodopa boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens generalizable rule representations in prefrontal cortex during the inference of meaning.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes and representations by which dopamine influences language processing remain unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers (n = 70, 47 females) boosts hippocampal processing and neural representations of generalizable abstract rules for successful inference of novel word meaning. We used a novel experimental paradigm that required participants to build new artificial word meanings by inferring and applying abstract affixation rules. A repetition suppression procedure was combined with multivariate representational similarity analyses to isolate the neural locus of both the abstract rules required for the compositional inference process, as well as the novel word meaning representations that were composed based on these abstract rules. Levodopa modulated not only inference-related signals in the hippocampal formation, but also abstract rule representations in the medial frontal cortex. These results support the hypothesis that dopamine boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of abstract rules when building novel meaning.Significance statement Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes by which dopamine boosts language processing have remained unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers enhances hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of generalizable abstract rules when building novel word meanings.

item.title: Capturing Habits in Humans: Neural Circuitry, Computations, and Clinical Mechanisms.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Habits allow repeated behaviors to be executed efficiently, but habitual control can contribute to maladaptive inflexibility when it dominates despite changing goals or consequences. This review examines recent advances in understanding habitual control across neural circuits, computation, clinical phenotypes, and measurement. We first consider dorsomedial striatal mechanisms that support action-outcome learning and flexible goal-directed behavior and how chronic stress can alter striatal inputs to bias learning toward habitual control. Progress on what computational reinforcement-learning accounts for arbitration between goal-directed and habitual systems is described along prefrontal mechanisms guiding model-based control, action perseveration, and compulsivity in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). A wider behavioral spectrum beyond action initiation is provided, reviewing emerging work on habitual inhibition and frontostriatal circuit dynamics of avoidance in OCD. Recent laboratory paradigms aim to reveal habit formation more sensitively than traditional outcome-devaluation paradigms, whereas real-world digital approaches use smartphones, wearables, and intensive longitudinal measurement to track habit formation and expression in everyday life. Integrating these approaches can help link habits to physiology, symptoms and neural circuits across laboratory to real-world and clinical contexts.

item.title: Janus in Thermosensation: The Dual Interoceptive-Exteroceptive Nature of Thermal Signals in Body Ownership.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Thermosensation has traditionally been studied for its essential role in survival, enabling detection of environmental thermal stimuli and the maintenance of thermal homeostasis. Interestingly, unlike most sensory systems, thermosensation provides information about both the external world and the body's internal physiological state. In this review, we conceptualize these two dimensions as exteroceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the thermal properties of external objects and the environment, and interoceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the body's thermal state. Growing evidence suggests that this dual nature serves functions that extend beyond survival and homeostasis. Alterations in both thermal perception and thermoregulation have been associated with changes in body ownership, the experience that one's body belongs to oneself, while manipulations of thermal signals can influence ownership itself. Here, we review the physiological and neural bases of exteroceptive and interoceptive thermosensation, from peripheral encoding to central processing, and examine their relationship with body ownership in healthy and clinical populations. We discuss evidence suggesting partially distinct yet potentially convergent neural substrates for these two dimensions of thermosensation, highlighting the insular cortex and its broader connectivity network as a candidate through which thermal information may sustain body ownership. Finally, we consider how emerging neurotechnologies offer new opportunities to investigate the contribution of thermosensation to body ownership while also opening novel avenues for neurorehabilitation. We propose that thermosensation represents an underexplored contributor to body ownership, opening new avenues for future research on how bodily and environmental thermal signals are integrated to support the sense of self.

item.title: Cross-Species Approaches to Understanding Human Cognition.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Recent methodological advances including high-density intracranial recordings and population-level analytical frameworks enable deeper and more direct integration between animal models and human neuroscience. As a result, there is an increasing need for standardized behavioral paradigms and circuit-level analyses that can be used in both animals and humans. Cross-species approaches provide crucial foundations for treating neurological and psychiatric disorders. Parallel experiments validate therapeutic targets and enable development of mechanistically grounded behavioral biomarkers for early disease detection. Here, we provide a brief review of recent findings that have direct implications for attention deficits, memory impairments, and decision-making dysfunctions. By linking mechanism to behavior, these approaches guide targeted interventions and effective clinical translation. While challenges remain, these integrated approaches are advancing our understanding of the mechanistic foundation of human cognition.

item.title: Revisiting Post-stimulus Theta Activity: Evidence for a Broadband Rather Than Narrowband Spectral Origin.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The aperiodic, 1/f -like component of electrophysiological activity is increasingly recognized as a meaningful feature of neural function rather than background noise. Meanwhile, many EEG studies interpret transient post-stimulus changes in oscillatory power as signatures of attention, salience, or cognitive control. Such interpretations typically depend on baseline normalization, which assumes aperiodic activity remains stable from pre- to post-stimulus periods. Using high-density EEG from typically developing children, we tested this assumption across two paradigms: an audiovisual simple reaction-time task (n = 36, 19 males and 17 females) and a visual oddball task (n = 38, 20 males and 18 females). In each, conventional spectral analyses were compared with analyses that explicitly modeled and removed aperiodic activity in both windows. Across tasks, stimulus onset produced robust increases in aperiodic exponent and offset, indicating systematic 1/f changes. In the audiovisual task these were modality specific, with central, parieto-occipital, or combined topographies by stimulus type. They diminished but persisted after event-related potential removal, suggesting they were not fully explained by phase-locked activity. Critically, once aperiodic activity was accounted for, the apparent theta increase was largely abolished in both tasks, including the canonical fronto-central enhancement to infrequent targets. The conventional method also overestimated beta desynchronization, especially in the induced signal, indicating a spurious consequence of spectral slope steepening. In contrast, alpha desynchronization remained robust and was enhanced, reflecting genuine suppression. Together, these findings suggest many conventional time-frequency effects, particularly apparent theta synchronization, may reflect stimulus-driven aperiodic changes rather than robust narrowband changes, challenging core assumptions of these analyses.

item.title: NeuroAI's Next Steps: Balancing Computation and Embodiment.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Deep neural networks trained at scale now predict neural activity across sensory cortices, raising a question that divides neuroscience: does the convergence between artificial and biological representations constitute understanding, or does understanding require models of biological processes grounded in the embodied, evolved character of natural intelligence? In this Dual Perspectives article, Bing Brunton and Patrick Mineault articulate two research programs-Process and Convergence-to engage this question about the future of NeuroAI research. The conversation is organized around four questions that probe what scaled model-brain alignment reveals, what the brain is coupled to and evolved to do, what success beyond the lab looks like, and where the field should invest over the coming decade. Their exchanges reveal the distance between the two programs to be primarily about the level of analysis and priorities for what to build next. The conversation converges on shared ground: measure broadly, then distill to causal principles.

item.title: Hormonal Effects during the Reproductive Years on Brain and Behavior: Molecular Discovery to Promising Therapeutics for Women's Mental Health.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Beginning at puberty and throughout the lifespan, women experience greater rates of depression, anxiety disorders, eating disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and hormone-linked mood disorders relative to men. How these disorders relate to hormonal fluctuations and associated changes in physiology and brain circuitry in women during the reproductive years is only partially understood. In this review, the molecular, structural, and functional brain changes during the reproductive years are discussed, with a specific focus on transitional changes during the perinatal period. Preclinical and clinical models of neuroplastic change are also discussed, along with neuromodulatory approaches that account for the contextual, spatial, and temporal parameters of interventions delivered during the postpartum period. Future directions may consider how hormonal fluctuations during reproductive years may improve preclinical and clinical models for women's mental health while acknowledging that greater work is needed to understand the role of a broader range of hormonal and environmental factors linked to mental health including lactation, trauma, contraceptive use, menstruation, and perimenopause.

item.title: Embodied Computation: How Does Embodiment Impact Sensorimotor and Cognitive Processing?
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Animals act on the world through a physical body and continually adjust behavior in response to the sensory feedback their actions produce. This closed loop between brain, body, and environment is central to motor control, but its role in other neural computations remains less clear. This review focuses on embodied computation: how the physical body shapes neural activity and behavior across functions ranging from motor control to cognitive processes. We examine the impact of embodiment in several domains, including compositional reuse, intrinsic motivation, metabolic costs, and connectome-constrained computation, with the broader aim of asking when the body can be abstracted away and when it is essential for explaining what the brain computes.

item.title: Hidden Vision and Beyond: Multiscale Foundations of Thalamic Organization.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The subcortical visual system is traditionally described through a small number of canonical pathways, with the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) viewed primarily as a first-order relay to primary visual cortex and additional routes through the superior colliculus, pulvinar and koniocellular LGN considered secondary or residual. Here, we review recent evidence across species, methods, and scales that challenge this framework and suggest that the visual thalamus is an active, dynamically regulated component of visual processing. We first consider primary and nonprimary visual pathways, showing how thalamic inputs shape cortical responses through the timing, spatial arrangement, synaptic organization, laminar targeting, and circuit-level integration of feedforward signals. We then reconsider the "first-order" status of LGN itself, reviewing evidence that nonretinal subcortical inputs, local inhibition, and corticothalamic feedback can alter LGN responses and the signals routed onward to cortex. This shifts the view of LGN from a passive relay supplying a dynamic cortex to a dynamically regulated node in its own right. Next, we review advances in higher-order thalamic organization, highlighting structured thalamocortical connectivity, network-level coordination, and state-dependent dynamics. Finally, we consider how thalamic functions change in the injured brain, where emerging models disentangle acute effects of damage from chronic compensation to reveal how surviving thalamic and downstream pathways may be remodeled, reweighted, or recruited to support residual visual function and recovery. Together, these findings support a multiscale view of the thalamus as a collection of specialized, adaptive nuclei embedded within distributed cortico-subcortical networks, with implications for perception, cognition, sensory disorders, and rehabilitation.

item.title: Six Challenges for a Mechanistic Science of Human Interoception.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Human interoception has become a major focus of systems, cognitive, and clinical neuroscience. Work across the past decade has shown that signals originating within the body shape perception, emotion, cognition, behavior, and health. Despite rapid methodological and conceptual progress, which substantially expanded our understanding of how bodily signals are processed and represented, much of the field remains constrained by descriptive methods. As these approaches passively assess bodily signals or subjective awareness, they have limited ability to establish causal mechanisms or translate interoceptive findings into clinically informative frameworks. Here, we identify six challenges and corresponding methodological directions for advancing human interoception research: strengthening integration of animal and human models, developing causal perturbation paradigms, capturing interoception in ecologically valid contexts, standardizing multidimensional measurement across bodily systems, adjudicating between computational accounts, and translating mechanistic insights into clinically informative models of health and disease. These challenges are best understood as linked requirements for moving interoception research from relevance to mechanism. Together, they highlight the need to move beyond predominantly static, passive, and single-modality approaches toward studies that can test how internal bodily signals relate to neural activity, behavior, and health.

item.title: Parallel Claustral Networks for Behavioral Control in Health and Disease.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The claustrum is among the most highly interconnected structures in the mammalian brain, with reciprocal projections spanning the cortical mantle and a growing roster of functions that range from sleep regulation to attentional control. Here we review current understanding of claustral circuit organization and function, synthesizing findings from anatomical, physiological, computational, and behavioral studies. We argue that a unifying logic underlies the apparent diversity of claustral functions: the claustrum operates through projection-defined subnetworks whose input selectivity, output targets, and local circuit interactions collectively determine their functional contribution and whose impact on cortical targets varies with arousal and ongoing brain state. Corticoclaustral connectivity is organized into matched input-output modules, local inhibitory circuits confer spatial filtering properties that amplify strong cortical signals while suppressing weaker ones and claustral output populations differ in their laminar targets, postsynaptic cell-type preferences, and molecular properties, producing diverse and context-dependent effects on cortical dynamics. These circuit properties translate into claustral regulation of cortical population dynamics across multiple timescales, from the moment-to-moment coordination of brain states to the consolidation of frontal control strategies. In pain and addiction, specific claustral projection populations are selectively dysregulated, and distinct subnetworks exert opposing influences on nociceptive sensitivity and drug-related behavior according to their cortical targets. Together, these findings position the claustrum as a modular subcortical hub for the selective regulation of distributed cortical networks and identify it as a candidate therapeutic target for disorders characterized by dysregulated cortical network activity, including chronic pain, addiction, and impulsivity.

item.title: Late Integration of Prior Expectations during Precision-Weighted Perceptual Decisions.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Adaptive perceptual decision-making relies on the ability to combine sensory evidence with prior expectations in a precision-weighted manner. Although Bayesian inference provides a clear normative account of how such integration should occur, the neural mechanisms through which the brain represents and combines priors and likelihoods remain poorly understood. Across two preregistered experiments, we investigated how the precision of learned priors and sensory likelihoods influence visual motion judgments and associated neural activity patterns during a random-dot motion estimation task. Neurotypical adult participants (N = 80, 58 female) reported directions of visual motion stimuli, with motion coherence varying randomly across trials. Prior expectations over the continuous motion direction space were manipulated block-wise by implicitly varying the probabilities with which different motion directions were presented. Consistent with precision-weighted inference, response accuracy improved as motion coherence increased with robust response biases toward the expected motion direction. Neural activity measured using electroencephalography (EEG) revealed reliable effects of prior expectation on the univariate central parietal positivity (CPP), consistent with reduced accumulation of sensory evidence under informative priors. Multivariate analysis using inverted-encoding models revealed robust effects of prior precision on stimulus-specific neural representations, but only late, during response planning stages. Together, these findings suggest that priors learned over a continuous space do not modulate the encoding of sensory evidence and are instead integrated later in the decision process.

item.title: Emotional Content Enhances Attentional Tracking of Conversations through Context-Sensitive Modulation of Auditory-Language Networks.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Engagement in conversation often requires continuous monitoring of relevant speech in a continuously evolving auditory environment. Emotional salience of semantic content may influence this process, but its role in attentional tracking of continuous speech remains unclear. We address this question using an audiovisual "cocktail-party" paradigm combined with source-localized magnetoencephalography and encoding-decoding analyses. Participants (18 females, 14 males) selectively attended to one dialogue while ignoring a concurrent distractor dialogue, with both emotional salience and semantic coherence of the conversations manipulated independently. Decoding analyses revealed that negatively valenced, high-arousal, and socially relevant semantic content strengthened neural speech tracking, but only for attended dialogues. This effect depended on semantic structure, emerging earlier in semantically coherent than incoherent dialogues. Encoding analyses further showed latency- and region-specific effects across temporal, parietal, and frontal cortical regions. Emotional salience and coherence jointly modulated midlatency (100-250 ms) responses, whereas late-latency (270-450 ms) responses were driven primarily by emotional salience. These findings demonstrate that emotional meaning enhances neural prioritization of attended speech and semantic coherence shapes the temporal dynamics of this enhancement. Together, these results indicate context-sensitive emotional modulation of auditory-language processing during selective listening of continuous speech.

item.title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics.
item.description:
PLoS computational biology
A central challenge in neuroscience is to understand how the brain flexibly balances local and distributed information processing to support diverse cognitive and conscious states. We hypothesize that a key signature of this balance is the presence of memory effects, which arise when a brain region's future activity depends not only on its current state, but also on past information fed back from the wider network. Here we introduce the FDTest, a method for assessing local memory effects in multidimensional systems by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT). We first apply this framework to whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging data, demonstrating that the brain's memory structure reflects its underlying connectivity. We then extend the analysis to individualized models of subjects during wakefulness and deep sleep. Memory effects are consistently stronger in wakefulness, indicating richer inter-regional dependencies and more integrated dynamics. These findings establish local memory as a dynamical marker of brain state and position the FDTest as a principled tool for probing the hidden structure of neural dynamics.

item.title: Semantic Processing in Unresponsive Patients With Acute Brain Injury.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Early prognostication after acute brain injury (ABI) is challenging because behavioral responsiveness may not accurately reflect preserved cognitive function. Neural responses to semantic incongruity can identify language processing despite the absence of overt behavior. We investigated whether bedside EEG could detect semantic processing in unresponsive patients with ABI and whether its presence was associated with long-term outcomes. Methods In this prospective 2-center cohort study, unresponsive adults with ABI admitted to neurologic intensive care units between 2022 and 2025 underwent bedside EEG during a language paradigm comparing congruent and incongruent sentence endings (e.g., "my favorite color is green/soon"). Semantic processing was defined by differential event-related responses within centroparietal channels (300-500 milliseconds) using cluster-based permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Outcomes were assessed for recovery of consciousness and functional recovery (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score ≥4) at 12 months by blinded interviewers. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, accuracy, and likelihood ratios. Results Among 105 patients (mean age 58 ± 19 years; 21% women; 53% Hispanic/Latino), the most common etiologies were intracerebral hemorrhage (45%), traumatic brain injury (43%), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (10%). Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy occurred in 31%. Semantic processing was detected in 13 patients (12%). Recovery of consciousness occurred in 77% of patients with semantic processing compared with 49% without semantic processing (odds ratio [OR] 3.5; 95% CI 0.9-13.5, p = 0.08). Functional recovery occurred in 42% with semantic processing compared with 14% without semantic processing (OR 4.5; 95% CI 1.2-16.6, p = 0.03). Semantic processing was highly specific but insensitive for predicting both recovery of consciousness (specificity 94%, sensitivity 18%) and functional recovery (specificity 92%, sensitivity 29%). After excluding patients who underwent withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy or died of non-neurologic medical complications, specificity increased to 100% for recovery of consciousness and 95% for functional recovery. Discussion EEG evidence of semantic processing can be detected in a subset of unresponsive patients with ABI during the acute phase of injury and is associated with favorable long-term outcomes. Semantic processing was a specific but insensitive biomarker of recovery, suggesting potential utility as a rule-in marker of preserved cognitive function. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multicenter cohorts before clinical implementation.

item.title: Brain Structural Changes in Blast-Exposed Special Operations Forces Soldiers.
item.description:
Journal of neurotrauma
Special Operations Forces (SOF) soldiers experience frequent low-level occupational blast exposure and mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), but the cumulative effects of these exposures on long-term neurological health remain poorly understood. The purpose of this longitudinal cohort study was to investigate associations between occupational blast exposure and brain structural change in SOF soldiers and to determine whether mTBI sustained between assessments moderated these associations. Male SOF soldiers (n = 88) underwent T1- and T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging at two timepoints. Volumetric segmentation was performed using FreeSurfer. Main outcomes were percent change in global brain tissue volumes, including cerebral cortex, cerebral white matter, lateral ventricles, subcortical gray matter, and cerebellar cortex. Exposure was quantified as months between Time 1 and Time 2, used as a proxy for cumulative occupational blast exposure during time in a high-tempo operational unit. The number of self-reported mTBIs sustained between timepoints was categorized as 0, 1-2, or 3 or more injuries. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied to control the false discovery rate. Greater occupational blast exposure predicted increased lateral ventricle percent change (F 1,86 = 9.86; B = 0.126%; R 2 = 0.103; p = 0.002; p -adjusted = 0.012) and decreased cerebellar cortex percent change (F 1,86 = 5.72; B = -0.074%; R 2 = 0.062; p = 0.019; p -adjusted = 0.047). Between-visit mTBI did not significantly moderate these associations. In this cohort of SOF soldiers, greater cumulative occupational blast exposure was associated with lateral ventricular expansion and cerebellar cortex volume loss. The rate of ventricular expansion observed in this study is atypical compared with expected change in healthy adults and may represent an early structural marker of blast-related brain vulnerability. Cerebellar cortex volume loss may reflect regional susceptibility to blast-related injury. Identifying brain structural changes associated with occupational blast exposure may help inform exposure-monitoring strategies and targeted interventions to preserve warfighter brain health and readiness.
